name: Gradual tanning lotion

lead: A gradual tanning lotion is a moisturizer or body lotion containing a small amount of a self-tanning agent, usually dihydroxyacetone (DHA). Used regularly, it deepens skin colour step by step, and a slight change is usually visible after the first application.

Users like it because slow build-up is less likely to leave streaks or an orange cast than a one-off self-tan. DHA is a simple sugar that reacts with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin in a browning reaction; the pigments are not melanin and form without UV light.

paras: People apply it like a daily body lotion, often for several days in a row until the shade they want, then continue every day or two to hold it. The colour fades over several days as the outer skin sheds, which is why it is reapplied.

Reported concerns centre on DHA: contact dermatitis, a possible increase in free-radical formation in sun-exposed skin soon after application, and no meaningful UV protection. Regulators approve DHA for external use and not for the eyes, lips or mucous membranes.

angle.text: Gradual tanning lotion builds a natural-looking tan over several days, with a slight colour change usually visible after the first use. The colour deepens with repeated daily application and does not protect against UV.

lead: A gradual tanning lotion, also called a build-up tanner, is a lotion or moisturizer that contains a mild self-tanning agent so that colour deepens with repeated daily use.[1] People use it to get a sun-kissed or healthier-looking skin tone without sun exposure. The gradual build lets them stop at the shade they want and reduces the streaks and orange patches associated with stronger one-off self-tanners.[1] Encyclopedic sources say a slight change in skin colour is usually visible after the first application and darkens with more frequent use.[1]

The most common active ingredient in sunless tanners is dihydroxyacetone (DHA), a three-carbon sugar that stains the outer skin layer through a browning (Maillard) reaction rather than by stimulating melanin.[1][2] Drugstore self-tanners typically contain 3 to 5 percent DHA, with the concentration adjusted for lighter or darker shades; professional products run higher.[1][2] Gradual lotions are generally formulated with less colour per application, though specific concentrations are not given in the sources.

Gradual lotions sit within a wider family that includes temporary bronzers, DHA creams and sprays, spray tans, tanning pills and injectables.[1] Regulatory and laboratory discussion centres on DHA and on the unlicensed melanotan peptides rather than on gradual lotions specifically, and no clinical studies of gradual tanning lotions as appearance products have been published.
infobox: Within hours; deepens over 24 to 72 hours and with repeated use[1][2]
DHA gives an SPF of about 3 per one summary[2]
DHA approved in the US for external use only[1]

paras: Sunless tanning is divided into several categories: temporary bronzers, DHA self-tanners, spray tans, tanning pills and injectable products.[1] Gradual lotions are described as a newer trend in which a moisturizer carries a small dose of tanning agent for use over multiple days, with colour rising slightly after the first use and darkening with more frequent use.[1]

Products are sold as body lotions and as facial moisturizers. Some blend DHA with erythrulose, a related sugar that develops colour more slowly.[1] Patent filings have also described formulations that combine tanning agents with natural plant pigments.[3] Temporary bronzers, by contrast, are powders, mousses, gels and lotions that wash off with soap and water and use ingredients such as walnut oil extract, jojoba extract or caramel; they can leave rub-off on clothes and look orangey and splotchy if applied unevenly.[1]

DHA concentration largely determines how dark a tan becomes: Wikipedia's article on DHA gives a range of 1 to 20 percent across products, with drugstore products usually 3 to 5 percent, professional products 5 to 20 percent and bronzers 1 to 15 percent. Darker, higher-concentration products give deeper colour in one coat but are more prone to streaking, which is the problem gradual lotions are designed to avoid.[2]

Spray tanning applies a DHA mist by hand or in booths and lasts about 5 to 10 days according to Wikipedia.[1] Oral tanning pills use carotenoids; the American Cancer Society says beta-carotene tanning pills may be harmful at the high doses used, and canthaxanthin, an approved food additive, is not approved for tanning, with pill use linked to hepatitis and retinopathy. Harmless carotenoderma, a yellowing of the skin, can take months to fade.[1] Unlicensed melanotan peptides are a separate category, described below.

German scientists recognised DHA as a skin-colouring agent in the 1920s after it stained skin during X-ray processing, and Eva Wittgenstein of Cincinnati Children's Hospital observed the effect in the 1950s while studying oral DHA treatment in children.[2][1] Man-Tan was the first commercial DHA self-tanner in 1959, followed by Coppertone's Quick Tan in 1960; both were criticised for orange colour and streaking, which hurt the category's reputation.[1][2]

Reformulations in the 1980s and 1990s produced more natural shades, automated spray-tan booths expanded the market in the late 1990s, and gradual products came later as a way to lessen streaking and uneven colour.[1][2] The FDA added DHA permanently to its list of approved cosmetic colour additives in the 1970s.[2] A 2019 analysis cited by Wikipedia reported increased US search interest in sunless tanning relative to tanning beds.[1]

DHA reacts with amino acid residues in keratin in the stratum corneum, forming brown compounds called melanoidins that resemble melanin in colour but arise without UV light and without involving melanocytes.[1][2] The reaction proceeds through a free-radical-mediated Maillard pathway as well as the conventional one.[1] Colour begins to appear in 2 to 4 hours, deepens over 24 to 72 hours, and fades as the outer cells are shed over roughly 3 to 10 days.[1][2] Injected DHA produces no pigmentation, which Wikipedia links to a role for oxygen in colour development.[2] Erythrulose works in a similar way but develops more slowly.[1]
DHA is chemically the simplest ketose, a hygroscopic white crystalline powder whose solutions are stable at pH 4 to 6 and degrade to brown products in more basic conditions.[2]

No studies found. Laboratory work on DHA has reported effects in cultured skin cells: a study from Bispebjerg Hospital found DNA damage, cell-cycle block and apoptosis in cultured keratinocytes, and a 2007 study led by Katinka Jung reported that free radicals in skin rose by more than 180 percent during sun exposure 40 minutes after treatment with 20 percent DHA compared with untreated skin.[1] These findings come from cell and tissue experiments and are debated, and the concentration used in the 2007 study is higher than in consumer gradual lotions.[1]

The US Food and Drug Administration approves DHA for application to the external skin and not for use around the eyes, on the lips, on mucous membranes or for inhalation, which can be hard to avoid in commercial spray booths.[1][2] Spray tans containing DHA have been linked to rashes, coughing, dizziness and fainting in the DHA article, which also associates frequent exposure with lung disease.[2] DHA and erythrulose can cause contact dermatitis, and fragrance in tanning lotions can trigger allergic or asthma reactions.[1] The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety concluded in 2010 that DHA spray tanning posed no risk, an opinion Wikipedia says critics said was shaped by industry-supplied evidence.[1]

A fake tan does not protect against UV. Some summaries state that DHA gives an SPF of about 3, and Wikipedia reports skin is especially susceptible to UV for about 24 hours after application; sunscreen added to tanners wears off faster than the colour does.[1][2] An FDA report cited by Wikipedia estimated that roughly 11 percent of applied DHA may reach living skin layers.[2] A pilot study suggests DHA-treated skin may inhibit vitamin D production.[1][2]

Unlicensed melanotan peptides, sold online and sometimes in gyms and salons as injectable tanning products, are a different route and are not sunless-lotion ingredients. Health agencies in Norway, Denmark, the UK, Ireland and the US have warned against them since 2007, and Wikipedia says they are not legal to sell for human use in any jurisdiction.[4][1]

In looksmaxxing forums, tanning is discussed mainly alongside tinted moisturizers, BB creams and bronzers as a way to look healthier and even out skin tone; forum users say these products give a more natural look than heavier foundation. The chain for gradual lotions is simple: a pale or uneven complexion is warmed with small daily layers of DHA colour, so face and body match and the shade can be stopped where the user likes it. Gradual lotions as such are rarely discussed by name in the forum threads reviewed, so community views specific to them are limited.
Related practices include tinted moisturizer, bronzer, spray tanning, and exfoliation before application, all of which are talked about in skin and grooming sections of appearance communities.

lore.intro: In appearance forums, sunless products are discussed as a way to look tanned and even-toned without UV, usually alongside tinted moisturizers and bronzers.

claims.claim: Building colour gradually avoids streaks and an orange cast.
A fake tan gives a healthier, more attractive look than pale or uneven skin.
A DHA tan protects you from the sun.
DHA is harmful because it generates free radicals.
Daily DHA use lowers vitamin D.
Tanning pills or melanotan are an easier alternative to lotions.
